card_summary: Saint Louis University’s Museum of Igorot Cultures and Arts focuses on Cordillera cultural heritage. Located at the university on Bonifacio Street, it is a different institution from UP Baguio’s Museo Kordilyera.
overview: ["SLU’s Museum of Igorot Cultures and Arts presents material relating to Igorot cultural heritage, including traditional objects and art. It is located at Saint Louis University on Bonifacio Street in Baguio. The museum’s educational purpose connects collections with the preservation and appreciation of culture, rather than treating the objects simply as decorations. Its visitor guidance asks guests not to handle artifacts without permission. Group and guided visits need advance arrangements with the museum. Travelers planning a focused cultural visit should distinguish this university institution from Museo Kordilyera at UP Baguio and the independently named Baguio Museum."]

card_summary: Mines View Park is an overlook on Baguio’s northeastern edge, looking toward Itogon and former mining landscapes. Its observation deck is reached by a winding stone-covered stairway, making the viewpoint a specific outdoor stop.
overview: ["Mines View Park occupies a promontory on the northeastern outskirts of Baguio. The outlook takes in the mining town of Itogon, including former gold and copper mining areas, with a glimpse toward the Amburayan Valley. The observation deck lies below a winding, stone-covered stairway near the parking area. That layout is worth considering when deciding which part of the park to visit; the park’s Baguio location and the landscape seen from it are not the same administrative place."]

card_summary: Taytay Boni, also called Puente de Boni, is an 1854 stone bridge in Miagao, Iloilo. Built for horse-drawn carriages, its yellow-coral-stone construction and prominent finial-topped posts make it a distinctive heritage stop.
overview: ["Taytay Boni was built in 1854 during the administration of Gobernadorcillo Miguel Navales. Its name remembers construction foreman Boni Neular, who came from Barangay Guibongan. The narrow bridge was intended for horse-drawn carriages and was constructed using tablea, or yellow coral stone, from the mountains of Igbaras and Miagao. The municipal history account describes large newel posts topped with pyramid-shaped finials, features that help explain the structure’s distinctive appearance. This is a particular bridge heritage site in Miagao, separate from a visit inside the parish church. Current access around the structure should be checked locally."]
